title: Dems' Dilemma: To Win Back Workers, Stop Talking About Democracy, Report Says
summary: For years, Democrats have sounded the alarm about threats to democracy. But a provocative new report suggests that message is falling flat with the very voters they need most: the working class. Titled 'The Left's Coalition Crisis,' the report — shared exclusively with NPR — draws on a survey of over 5,000 Americans to reveal a stark priority gap between college-educated liberals and working-class voters of all races. While liberal graduates rank 'resisting authoritarianism' as their second-highest concern, working-class voters place it 19th out of 20 issues. 'If we really care about stopping authoritarianism, we have to stop talking about defending democracy in the way that we've been doing,' said co-author Jared Abbott, who holds a Ph.D. from Harvard and leads the Center for Working Class Politics. The report's other author, law professor Joan C. Williams, put it bluntly: 'I am tired of losing.' Both are progressives who want their party to win. Their prescription? Embrace a populist message that decries a 'rigged economy' where hard work fails to yield a stable middle-class life. Focus relentlessly on paychecks, prices, and personal safety. And crucially, avoid any hint of looking down on Americans without college degrees. The report points to Kamala Harris's 2024 campaign, which centered on defending democracy and abortion access — two issues that energize the college-educated base but don't resonate with workers. The lesson, they argue, isn't that working-class voters are unreachable. It's that you can't reach them if you're not speaking to their daily struggles. 'It's about understanding that people need a sense of personal and economic security before they will support the changes progressives are calling for,' the authors write. For a party still reeling from electoral losses, the message is clear: respect and relevance must come before rhetoric.
why_it_matters: This story reveals how political messages that seem urgent to some can feel completely out of touch to others. For a teenager beginning to form their own views, it shows why listening to different experiences — not just loud voices in one bubble — is crucial for a healthy democracy, and how economic fairness is often a deeper concern than abstract ideals.

background_read: The Democratic Party has struggled to hold onto working-class voters for decades. In 2016, Donald Trump won many of these voters with promises to bring back manufacturing jobs and fix 'rigged' trade deals. This shift highlighted a growing divide between college-educated liberals who often live in cities and working-class Americans who may feel left behind. Jared Abbott of the Center for Working Class Politics — an organization that studies how economic class shapes voting — argues that unless Democrats change their language, they will keep losing. Joan C. Williams, a prominent law professor and author, has written widely about class divides and how progressives sometimes unintentionally look down on people without degrees. Kamala Harris's 2024 presidential run as the Democratic nominee focused heavily on protecting democracy and reproductive rights, but exit polls showed these issues did not sway many working-class households as much as pocketbook concerns. This tension is not new: in past elections, candidates like Bill Clinton and Barack Obama used economic appeals ('It's the economy, stupid') to build broader coalitions.

The phrase 'rigged economy' has become a staple of populist rhetoric, used not only by left-leaning figures like Bernie Sanders but also by right-wing politicians. Critics say that simply changing the message is not enough; policies like raising the minimum wage, investing in job training, and lowering healthcare costs must follow. The survey of 5,000 Americans provides data backing the idea that many working-class people feel that talk about democracy sounds abstract when they are worried about rent and groceries. This creates a dilemma: how can a party warn about authoritarian threats while not sounding alarmist to those struggling day to day?
Article_Structure: LEAD: A new report says Democrats' focus on threats to democracy is backfiring with working-class voters.
└─ SOURCE: 'The Left's Coalition Crisis,' based on a survey of 5,000 Americans.
THE DATA GAP: College-educated liberals rank 'resisting authoritarianism' as their second concern; working-class voters place it 19th out of 20 issues.
VOICES OF CHANGE: Co-authors Jared Abbott and Joan C. Williams push for a different approach.
├─ ABBOTT: Stop defending democracy the way they have been; winning requires a new pitch.
└─ WILLIAMS: 'I am tired of losing' — signaling electoral frustration as a progressive.
THE PRESCRIPTION: Adopt a populist economic message about a rigged economy, paychecks, and personal safety.
├─ KEY: Avoid condescension toward those without college degrees.
└─ EXAMPLE: Harris's 2024 campaign stressed democracy and abortion — issues that energized educated base but didn't resonate with workers.
UNDERLYING LESSON: Working-class voters are reachable, but only if politicians speak directly to their daily struggles for security.
CLOSING NOTE: For a party 'reeling' from defeats, respect and relevance must come before rhetoric.

perspectives.description: If Democrats heed this advice, they could rebuild a broad coalition that includes working-class voters of all races, making the party more competitive in swing states and blue-collar regions. A focus on pocketbook issues might also produce policies that genuinely lift families out of poverty, which would strengthen democracy by giving more people a stake in the system.

Some worry that downplaying threats to democracy could backfire, allowing undemocratic behavior to grow unchecked. Others fear that 'rigged economy' talk can cross into empty populism that blames minorities or immigrants, or that it might alienate socially liberal donors who fund campaigns. There is also the risk that voters could see the shift as opportunistic rather than sincere.

The survey data offers a snapshot of how education level and daily economic pressure shape political priorities. This pattern — with cultural issues like 'authoritarianism' landing much higher among graduates — reflects a long-term realignment where the Democratic coalition has tilted toward educated voters while losing support among some working families. Researchers caution that messaging is only part of the solution; structural economic changes may be needed.

The report urges an immediate change in rhetoric, but lasting success would likely depend on policy wins: higher wages, cheaper healthcare, and visible improvements in safety. If Democrats can blend a strong economic pitch with a hopeful vision, they might not only win back working-class voters but also reinvigorate faith in democratic institutions. The 2028 election cycle will test whether the party truly reshapes its message or slips back into a college-educated comfort zone.
